Commentary.Commentary: We are back with the chase. Amy Jones and Tammy Beaumont are opening the innings for England Women, while Rosemary Mair is getting ready to bowl the first over for New Zealand Women. The deck is offering something to the bowlers who are willing to vary their pace and lengths. Let's see how England starts their pursuit of the target. Sophie Devine leads her side for the final time in ODI cricket for New Zealand Women.
... The Run Chase ...

We can take that as a final word from Sir Bishop. This pitch is certainly tricky to bat upon but 168 looks too small a total to challenge the stronger batting lineup of England Women. New Zealand Women seem to be around 50-60 runs short but you never know in this sport - take 3-4 quick wickets and get into that out-of-form English middle order and try and force a collapse. We are not too far away from the resumption as Tammy Beaumont has already made her way to the English team's dugout downstairs, waiting for her batting partner. Please stay tuned.

PITCH REPORT 2.0 - Easy peasy for England Women? May not be that easy but cetainly not difficult, feels former West Indian champion IAN BISHOP. He observes the deck now and admits that in the morning, it looked like one where runs will flow. But as things went on, the balls started to slow up and started to keep low. Ian informs that there are some footmarks on the pitch which should assist the spinners but the New Zealand bowlers will have to work really hard to defend this total.

England's ALICE CAPSEY is up for a chat with the broadcasters. Capsey expresses her satisfaction with contributing to the team's success by picking up wickets and restricting the opposition to a low total. On being asked about the deck, Alice reckons that the pitch slowed down after the Powerplay and described her approach as attacking the stumps with some variations. Capsey also mentioned that the pitch kept low, which likely aided her bowling. Regarding the chase, she acknowledges that no target is easy but expresses optimism.

Not a great bowling discipline by England but they will not mind it. They have got the job done. Or at least, set themselves up for a win. They were very sloppy with the ball and on the field, bowling too many loose deliveries and even dropped a catch of Izzy Gaze. But it just seemed that it was their day as they finally hit their lines and lengths post the 25th over mark. Linsey Smith, after struggling to grip the ball for her first ball, ended up with 3 wickets while Dean, Capsey and Ecclestone supported her well. There was a bit of a fright in the English camp with Sophie Ecclestone walking off the field, injuring her bowling shoulder, her left. She did not even bowl a complete over, as a precaution to rest before the semifinal and that's a positive for Nat Sciver-Brunt - despite Ecclestone bowling just 4 legal balls, her young spinners took 6/85 in 22.2 overs combined. But having said that, the entire nation of England will be praying that the left-arm champion recovers fully before Wednesday.

The scorecard does not reflect too well for the batters, with only 3 batters crossing 20 but none reaching the 50-mark. No one looked settled at the crease on a pitch which looks way different from the one that hosted the India-Australia match. The pitch looked dry and the balls were stopping and coming onto the batters. So the timing was off and there was never really much efficient strokeplay for too long a time. England Women resorted to their cutters and change of pace pretty quickly and 7 of the 9 wickets picked by bowlers were taken by spinners.

It was a pretty bizarre innings to be honest. England Women started off poorly with the ball and in fact, were poor for near 70 percent of the innings. But New Zealand Women were not too great either, unable to capitalize on the freebies being offered. They lost Suzie Bates early but Georgia Plimmer and Amelia Kerr got the tide flowing with a fine 68-run stand for the second wicket. However, once the stand was broken and Amelia departed, it appeared to take a Domino effect and from 89/1, the innings stumbled to 168.

70 balls not used by New Zealand Women. They had scored 89 in the first 113. Who would have thought that would end up playing just a shade over 38 overs? They were 89/1 at one stage, but ended up losing 9/79 in the next 117 balls. And as it turns out, this is New Zealand's lowest score in this World Cup, their first sub-200 score in a proper WODI since 24th October 2024 - that's a good 12 months and 10 innings prior!

The ball catches the shoulder of the bat and travels over mid off, but Charlie Dean keeps her eyes on the ball, runs back and takes a fantastic catch over her head. Tahuhu departs for 2 (8) and NEW ZEALAND WOMEN ARE BOWLED OUT FOR 168!

OUT! CAUGHT BEHIND! Not out was the verdict from the umpire, not out was the verdict from the fielder running in from square leg but dear me, what a brilliant piece of review! On a length, outside off, Sophie Devine came on the front foot and looked to drive this down the ground. But the ball just shaped in a touch after pitching and beat the batter, at least, that is what we all felt initially. The keeper, Amy Jones, upto the stumps, took the ball superbly and put in an appeal for the catch but the umpire shook her hand. The keeper and bowler got together and eventually, NSB signalled for the review. While the English players got together, someone came running in from square leg and shouted, 'That's not out, no edge'. But what does technology say? UltraEdge detects a spike as the ball is near the inside edge and the onfield decision is overturned! 'THANK YOU, SOPHIE' is what Katey Martin says on air, to one of the best servants of New Zealand cricket. A fine 23 (35) in her final outing, but sadly, her team is in a sorry state again. 89/1 at one stage and 155/6 now.

Commentary.Commentary: DRINKS BREAK. Time for a refreshment for all and think about how the game has panned so far and how can it get better. It has been a pretty bizarre game so far, with neither side playing its best cricket. England Women have picked up a wicket, but that too thanks to Lady Luck, with New Zealand Women failing to capitalize on some loose bowling. The White Ferns, on the other hand, have their run rate at around 5 an over, but nearly 65 percent of their innings has gone in dot balls. They have one good news though - SOPHIE ECCLESTONE IS BACK ON THE FIELD. Given that she went off for a physical injury, she should be able to bowl immediately, but the question is - should she? OUT! CAUGHT! Wow, New Zealand Women have been struggling to make use of freebies and this one has actually resulted in a wicket. Linsey Smith has been struggling to grip the ball, not sure why. Whether it is because of the wetness from the covers or something else, not sure, but she has just been dishing up full tosses and luckily for her, none of them have been punished. And this one is an icing on the cake. She bowls a high full toss, outside off, Suzie Bates looks to hit it over mid off but just cannot time it properly, as the ball arrives slowly. It was actually misdirected, as the ball slipped out of Smith's hand and came dipping through to Bates, very slowly. The ball went off the toe end of the bat towards mid off where the substitute, Emma Lamb, on for Sophie Ecclestone, makes no mistake. Smith cannot believe her luck and Bates starts to walk off, but is made to wait as the umpires want to check the height of that ball. Technology is used to track the flight of the ball and it shows the ball to be dipping, making contact with the bat well below Bates' waist. Bates has to resume walking now, as she departs for 10 (16) and New Zealand Women are 21/1 after 5.3 overs!

Commentary.Commentary: Right. The anthems have been done and we are ready for the first and last double header of this mega event to get us underway on this mega Sunday. Might be a couple of dead rubbers, but will be no less entertaining, especially this first match. The English team is in a huddle. England would want to win this match and finish second. What's the difference if you finish second or third, do you ask? Well, just in case, just in case, the first semifinal is washed out in Guwahati, the team ranked higher goes through. So 2 is better than 3, right? Time for this game to begin then. The New Zealand Women openers make their way out to the middle - Suzie Bates and Georgia Plimmer. It will be Lauren Bell to start things off against Bates. Here we go!
It is time for the national anthems. The players and the umpires line up for the same. It will be the Kiwi anthem first, followed by that of England.

PITCH REPORT - Former West Indian cricketer IAN BISHOP informs us that the weather is fine in Visakhapatnam, with the temperature reading 31 degrees but adds that the humidity percentage of 80 is very high. Also says that the dimensions down the ground read 67 metres, which is very big for a Women's game. Adds that the square dimensions are relatively shorter, around 55-57 metres, so expect a lot of sweeps and reverse sweeps. For West Indies Women's cricketer, STACY ANN KING, is observing the deck. Calls the surface as a very good one, predicting it to be full of runs. Informs that this is the same deck which was used for the India-Australia match, where we saw 331 being chased down by the Aussies. Adds that the surface looks very strong with a little bit of cracks. Ends by saying that it is a very good pitch for batting with the bowlers getting something eventually, but not the seamers.

The skipper of England, NAT SCIVER-BRUNT, says that England wanted to bat as well. But adds that now given that they will be bowling first, will look to make the most of that and try to restrict New Zealand to a small total. On the surface, Sciver-Brunt feels that the track looks a bit dry and might be a bit slow which is why she wanted to bat first. On the team news, Nat informs that Emma Lamb makes way for Danni Wyatt-Hodge. On being asked whether it is right to make the change now, ahead of the semi-final one, NSB sounds positive, though admitting that it is pretty tough ahead of the semifinal but believes that Wyatt-Hodge is pretty experienced and will slot in straightaway in the semifinal. On Sophie Devine, who will be playing her last WODI today, Nat Sciver-Brunt calls her a formidable opponent and jokes that it will be a relief for bowlers as they will not have to bowl to her anymore after this game.

The captain of New Zealand, SOPHIE DEVINE, cities that her reason to bat first is the good-looking wicket to post a big total. Devine expresses her team's inconsistency, stating they've played well in patches and need to convert partnerships into big scores. She emphasizes the importance of keeping the stumps in play while bowling and acknowledges that there have already been some tears in the team. Devine also shares her desire to enjoy the game and have fun with her teammates, savoring the experience of her final ODI.

England Women (Playing XI) - Tammy Beaumont, Amy Jones (WK), Heather Knight, Nat Sciver-Brunt (C), Alice Capsey, Danni Wyatt-Hodge (IN FOR EMMA LAMB), Sophia Dunkley, Charlie Dean, Sophie Ecclestone, Linsey Smith and Lauren Bell.

The match promises to be an exciting encounter, with both teams looking to achieve different goals. England Women will look to build on their strengths and prepare for the semifinals, while New Zealand Women will aim to give their fans a memorable farewell to Sophie Devine's illustrious career. Can England use this match to prepare for the semifinals and find their winning rhythm? Or will New Zealand, led by Devine's determination, pull off a win and send their legend off in style? The stage is set for an exciting match between two teams with different motivations. Stay tuned for toss and team updates.

For New Zealand Women, this match holds special significance as it could be the last 50-over World Cup for three of their legendary cricketers, including captain Sophie Devine, Lea Tahuhu and Suzie Bates. New Zealand's campaign has been marred by rain and inconsistency. Devine has been the standout performer, and her team will be keen to give its departing legend a fitting farewell. With nothing to lose, New Zealand can play freely, and Devine will undoubtedly be looking to leave a lasting impression and end her 50-over career on a high note. It has been a below-par tournament for Amelia Kerr, Georgia Plimmer and Maddy Green as well and they'll be itching to get the act right finally.

England Women, already assured of a semifinal spot where they'll be playing against South Africa Women, look to conclude the league stage on a winning note. The English team, led by Nat Sciver-Brunt, has been impressive, with standout performances from the skipper herself, Heather Knight, Amy Jones and Sophie Ecclestone. England might consider rotating the squad by giving Tammy Beaumont a rest and promoting Danni Wyatt-Hodge. Still, the focus will be on maintaining momentum ahead of their semifinal clash.

A warm welcome to everyone around the globe. England Women take on New Zealand Women in the penultimate league match at the Dr. Y. S. Rajasekhara Reddy ACA–VDCA Cricket Stadium in Visakhapatnam. For England Women, this match serves as a crucial warmup ahead of the semifinals, where they'll look to fine tune their preparations and build momentum. After a strong start to the tournament, England have shown some inconsistency, and this match provides the perfect opportunity to rediscover their best form. Whereas for New Zealand Women, they would want to win this and end the tournament by bringing a wide smile to the faces of their fans.

England Women and New Zealand Women are set to face off in the first game of a double header on Sunday, a match that, although inconsequential in terms of qualification, holds significance for the teams' semifinal seeding. A win for England could propel them to second place, pitting them against the loser of the Australia-South Africa match in the semifinals. The English team has navigated the tournament with solidity, but their batting has been a mixed bag, with Amy Jones, Nat Sciver-Brunt, and Heather Knight consistently delivering while the rest of the lineup has struggled to find consistency. Their bowlers, however, have been reliable, picking up crucial wickets at pivotal moments, which raises the question of whether the team will stick with their winning formula or introduce some fresh legs ahead of the semifinals. On the other hand, New Zealand Women will be looking to end their campaign on a high note, despite being eliminated from contention. Their tournament was marred by a slow start and rain-affected matches, and their batting lineup, apart from the skipper Sophie Devine, has been inconsistent. Key players like Suzie Bates and Amelia Kerr have underperformed, while Brooke Halliday and Izzy Gaze have been a beacon of hope. With nothing to lose, New Zealand might look to give their younger players some valuable game time, although it might be too little, too late in the tournament. Will England Women climb to the second spot or will the White Ferns end the tournament on a high and with some pride? We shall have the answer soon.
